title: Chapter 109 — Ahab and Starbuck in the Cabin
paragraphs: As usual, they were pumping out the ship the next morning, and, surprisingly, a fair amount of oil came up with the water; the casks down below must have sprung a bad leak. Everyone was very worried, and Starbuck went down to the cabin to report this bad news.*

*In sperm-whalers with any considerable quantity of oil on board, it is a regular twice-weekly duty to run a hose into the hold and drench the casks with sea-water, which is afterward removed at varying intervals by the ship's pumps. In this way the aim is to keep the casks damp and tight; while from the changed character of the water pumped out, the sailors readily detect any serious leakage in the precious cargo.

By now the Pequod was approaching Formosa and the Bashee Isles from the south and west; between them runs one of the tropical passages out of the China seas into the Pacific. So Starbuck found Ahab with a general chart of the eastern archipelagoes spread out in front of him, along with a separate one showing the long eastern coasts of the Japanese islands of Nippon, Matsumae and Shikoku. The wondrous old man, with his back to the gangway door, his snow-white new ivory leg braced against the screwed-down leg of his table and a long jackknife like a pruning-hook in his hand, was frowning and tracing out his old courses again.
"Who's there?" hearing the footstep at the door, but not turning round to it. "On deck! Begone!"
"Captain Ahab is mistaken; it is I. The oil in the hold is leaking, sir. We must hoist the Burtons (the hoisting tackles) and break out the hold."
"Hoist the Burtons and break out? Now that we are nearing Japan — heave to here for a week to tinker a parcel of old hoops?"
"It's either that, sir, or lose more oil in one day than we can make up in a year. Something we sail twenty thousand miles to get is worth saving, sir."
"So it is, so it is; if we get it."
"I was speaking of the oil in the hold, sir."

"And I wasn't speaking or thinking of that at all. Get out! Let it leak! I'm all leaks myself. Yes! Leaks within leaks! Not only full of leaky casks, but those leaky casks are in a leaky ship; and that's a far worse fix than the Pequod's, man. Yet I don't stop to plug my leak, for who can find it down in the deep-loaded hull? And even if it were found, how could anyone hope to plug it in this life's howling gale? Starbuck! I won't have the Burtons hoisted."
"What will the owners say, sir?"

"Let the owners stand on Nantucket beach and outyell the typhoons. What does Ahab care? Owners, owners? You are always prattling to me, Starbuck, about those miserly owners, as if the owners were my conscience. But look here, the only real owner of anything is its commander; and listen, my conscience is in this ship's keel. On deck!"

"Captain Ahab," said the mate, flushing as he stepped farther into the cabin. His boldness was so oddly respectful and careful that it almost seemed not only to be trying in every way to avoid the slightest outward show of itself, but also, inwardly, to be more than half unsure of itself. "A better man than I am might well overlook in you what he would be quick enough to resent in a younger man — yes, and in a happier one, Captain Ahab."
"Devils! Do you then so much as dare to think critically of me? On deck!"
"No, sir, not yet; I do beg you. And I do dare, sir — to be patient! Shall we not understand each other better than we have till now, Captain Ahab?"

Ahab seized a loaded musket from the rack — forming part of most South Sea vessels' cabin furniture — and pointing it toward Starbuck, exclaimed: "There is one God that is Lord over the earth, and one Captain that is lord over the Pequod. On deck!"

For an instant in the flashing eyes of the mate, and his fiery cheeks, you would have almost thought that he had really received the blast of the leveled barrel. But, mastering his emotion, he half-calmly rose, and as he left the cabin, paused for an instant and said: "You have outraged, not insulted me, sir; but for that I ask you not to beware of Starbuck — you would only laugh; but let Ahab beware of Ahab. Beware of yourself, old man."

"He grows brave but nevertheless obeys; that's a most careful bravery!" murmured Ahab, as Starbuck disappeared. "What's that he said — Ahab beware of Ahab — there's something there!" Then, unconsciously using the musket for a walking stick, with an iron brow he paced to and fro in the little cabin; but presently the thick furrows of his forehead relaxed, and returning the gun to the rack, he went to the deck.

"You are only too good a fellow, Starbuck," he said quietly to the mate; then, raising his voice to the crew: "Furl the topgallant-sails, and close-reef the topsails, fore and aft; back the main-yard; hoist the Burton, and break out in the main-hold."

It would perhaps be useless to guess exactly why Ahab acted this way toward Starbuck. It may have been a flash of honesty in him; or mere prudent policy which, under the circumstances, sternly forbade the slightest sign of open disaffection, however fleeting, in the important chief officer of his ship. However it was, his orders were carried out; and the Burtons were hoisted.
